prompt: Your PM keeps declining your requests to spend time on refactoring. How do you make the case?
answer_markdown: Stop asking in engineering language. 'Messy', 'legacy', and 'a nightmare' all translate to a stakeholder as 'the engineer has an aesthetic preference', and meanwhile they are fielding requests backed by revenue numbers. Translate the debt into one of four currencies the business already tracks: engineering time, incidents, revenue at risk, or hiring and ramp-up time. Concretely, 'the auth module is spaghetti' becomes 'every auth change costs three days instead of one, we made nine of them last quarter, that is eighteen wasted engineer-days, and two of last quarter's SEV2s originated there.' Get the change count from git rather than guessing, because a number that gets challenged and turns out to be invented sinks the entire case. Then attach it to a trigger — nobody funds refactoring in the abstract, but almost everybody funds it immediately after an incident it caused, or as part of a funded feature that has to be built on top of it.

prompt: Tell me about technical debt you decided NOT to fix.
answer_markdown: This is the strongest senior signal in the whole topic, because anyone can advocate for refactoring and knowing when it is waste is far rarer. Two tests produce good answers. The interest test: debt only charges you where you keep working, so genuinely ugly code in a stable module that changes twice a year and has caused no incidents costs you approximately nothing, and cleaning it spends the team's scarcest resource for no return. The deletion test: if the code is scheduled for replacement or decommissioning, improving it is pure loss regardless of how bad it is. A strong answer also covers how you handled the person who wanted to do it — say the reason rather than just the no, name the condition that would change your mind ('if the vendor migration slips past a year, this changes'), and redirect their energy to a high-interest area instead, because the frustration is legitimate even when the request is wrong.

prompt: What does Martin Fowler's technical debt quadrant let you say that 'we had a lot of tech debt' doesn't?
answer_markdown: The quadrant splits debt on two axes — deliberate versus inadvertent, and prudent versus reckless — which lets you distinguish four situations that call for completely different responses. Deliberate and prudent ('we must ship now and deal with the consequences') is a legitimate business decision you should defend rather than apologise for. Inadvertent and prudent ('now we know how we should have done it') is unavoidable, because you learn a domain by building in it. Only the two reckless quadrants are actual failures, and even they need different fixes: deliberate-reckless is a process and review problem, while inadvertent-reckless is a training and mentoring problem. The practical value in an interview is precision — saying 'we took deliberate prudent debt to hit the launch and wrote down what we traded' demonstrates judgement, whereas 'the codebase had a lot of debt' describes weather.

prompt: You joined six months ago and want a two-month rewrite of the payments integration. Your director says no — the roadmap is full and she's heard this from two previous engineers. What now?
answer_markdown: Stop asking for the rewrite, because her objection is rational and a better slide deck addresses none of it. A two-month rewrite of the payment path is a large unhedged bet with no incremental value, proposed by someone with six months of context, and she has been burned by the same request twice. Break it into pieces that each deliver value alone and can each be abandoned without waste: characterisation tests around current behaviour first, which takes about a week and makes every subsequent change safer immediately, then extract one retry path, then the next seam. Then attach the first piece to funded work — the next payments feature becomes 'this feature, plus tests for the code it touches, is three weeks instead of two', so nobody has to approve a rewrite at all. This also builds the track record that makes your next ask credible, which is the real constraint here: the two previous engineers asked and left, and she is pattern-matching on that.

prompt: A shortcut you deliberately took nine months ago is now blocking a customer deal, and in the meeting someone asks 'who built it this way?'
answer_markdown: Own it flatly and immediately reframe to the decision rather than the person: 'I did, deliberately, to hit the March launch — here is what it bought us and here is what it costs now.' Deliberate prudent debt is not a mistake and you should not perform contrition for it, because over-apologising teaches everyone watching that shortcuts are shameful, which produces a team that either hides them or refuses to take them at all. Both outcomes are worse than the debt. Then move straight to the number: what unblocking this deal costs in engineer-days versus what the deal is worth. That converts an awkward accountability moment into a decision the room can make, which is the actual job. The reason interviewers like this scenario is that both naive responses — defensiveness and excessive apology — make the conversation about you rather than about the trade-off.

prompt: How do you stop technical debt accumulating in the first place?
answer_markdown: Weak answers appeal to discipline — 'we should all care more about quality' — which fails because debt accumulates from rational local decisions under deadline pressure, not from carelessness. Strong answers are structural. Log debt at the moment it is taken, with the reason and what it would cost to repay, so it is visible rather than folklore. Put the things that erode first into the definition of done, particularly tests, since they are what gets silently dropped when a deadline moves. Consider a standing allocation — some fixed fraction of each sprint — so paydown does not require winning an argument every single time, which is where most teams fail. And note the asymmetry worth mentioning: the goal is not zero debt, because deliberate prudent debt is a genuinely useful tool. The goal is that every piece of debt is a choice someone made knowingly rather than something that accumulated while nobody was looking.
